criteria.evidence: #10: "Your level: B1". Against trueBand A2, placement is near (distance 1), not the exact A2 this criterion requires.

#2: "Where do you see or hear English in your life?" receives a relevant answer. All five tasks receive appropriate responses. At #8, "compare is difficult for me", but she nevertheless compares both options; this shows production difficulty rather than misunderstanding the instructions.

#8: "Sorry, I don't know how to say" is followed by another practical task at #9 without reprimand. The recorded task verdict attributes difficulty to "basic grammar", not her admission. Explicit reassurance or a response to a repeat request is not demonstrated.
#5–#9 show placement tasks; no six-topic selection is shown.
No conversation moments are recorded. #10 provides only the next focus: "Practise using clear, accurate sentences to help guests in new situations."

#5–#9 cover water, a cold room, noise, sightseeing and a forgotten bag. #9: "tell them what you can do to help and why". Nothing shown is adult content, humiliating or a request for sensitive personal data.

judgeAgreement.disagreements: None. #5 and #6 select the correct replies. #7 correctly identifies both listening details; grammar errors do not negate comprehension. #8 does not demonstrate B2 production. #9 provides a connected, comprehensible plan consistent with a B1 task pass, despite errors. Task-level agreement does not establish confidence in the overall band.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears. #9's room-number request is learner-authored dialogue in a fictional hotel scenario.

findings.title: The verdict smooths over mixed evidence
findings.expected: A credible near placement explains the difference between understanding guests, using familiar phrases and handling unfamiliar speech.
findings.got: B1 is reported with high confidence in the facts and a consistency claim on screen, despite an A2 production observation. Petra remains doubtful.
findings.evidence: #7's recorded assessment says "small grammar errors ... kept your English at A2 here". #10 says "your answers agreed with each other". Petra reacts: "B1 is higher than I think, because on phone I still don't understand sometimes."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Explain the mixed skill evidence and uncertainty in plain language; avoid claiming agreement without reconciling the A2 observation with B1.

findings.title: The next focus is too general to act on
findings.expected: A teacher-like next step tied to her demonstrated difficulty and stated goal.
findings.got: The focus mentions guests but offers no specific sentence pattern, example or phone-comprehension practice.
findings.evidence: #4: "And phone call is difficult for me." #10: "Practise using clear, accurate sentences to help guests in new situations."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Give one concrete next exercise or useful phrase grounded in her answers, such as practising a guest complaint over the phone.

findings.title: A short, understandable route reaches the result
findings.expected: Complete the check independently with at most five tasks and low pressure.
findings.got: Three introductory questions and five tasks lead directly to the verdict; no retry or outside help appears.
findings.evidence: #2: "You can answer in English or your own language." #5–#9: "Some are easy and some are hard". #10 reaches "Your level: B1".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve the five-task limit, clear progression and explicit permission to use her own language.

findings.title: Hotel scenarios make the check relevant
findings.got: Tasks use guest requests and realistic service problems, helping Petra engage despite anxiety.
findings.evidence: #6: "The room is cold." Petra says, "I know this phrase from the hotel, so I feel a little calmer." #9 asks how to help retrieve a bag from a closed café.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve realistic hospitality scenarios while distinguishing familiar service phrases from broader speaking ability.

judge.voice: I would try it again because the hotel questions felt useful. The cold room and forgotten bag are problems I understand, and I did not feel laughed at when I struggled. Nothing shown worried me as a parent, although I have not seen the children's practice. B1 surprised me. I can say familiar sentences at reception, but unexpected phone calls are still difficult. I wanted the result to explain that difference. The advice to use clear, accurate sentences does not tell me what to practise tomorrow. I cannot judge the corrections yet because this was only the level check. The short route felt manageable, but I cannot say how much time it saved or whether the waits were worthwhile from this record. I would tell a colleague it is worth trying for hotel English, with some caution about trusting the level.
